title: Late Haas F1 call-up in Mexico 'dream come true' – Hirakawa
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa has reflected on his late call-up to race for Haas at the Mexico City Grand Prix, the Japanese driver describing the chance to make his Formula 1 debut as a "dream come true".

Hirakawa was called up by Haas just hours before Qualifying on Saturday in Mexico to replace regular driver Esteban Ocon, with the team offering no further comment on the reasons for the switch.

Hirakawa had already competed in Free Practice 1 on Friday for the American team in his role as reserve driver and to comply with the regulations, citing that every full-time racer must make way for a rookie twice in the season.

Hirakawa's outing on Friday was his ninth appearance in an FP1 session after previous running for Haas, Alpine and McLaren since 2024, but he will make his first Grand Prix start on Sunday after qualifying in P19.

"Obviously was a very big surprise this morning but I'm always here to be a reserve driver," said Hirakawa when asked about the details for the call-up, having also driven in FP3.

"This is a role for myself, I was ready but always dreaming about it. Today, dream come true. Qualifying today, race tomorrow.

"Just these 12 hours passed so fast, have so much to prepare and the team helped a lot for myself. Really thanks to the team."

A driver for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship (WEC), Hirakawa is a two-time champion in the category, as well as winning the 2022 Le Mans 24 Hours.

Hirakawa is also in contention to win the WEC next weekend at Monza, with any decision about who will race for Haas in Brazil next weekend yet to be confirmed.

Despite not knowing if this might be his only F1 outing, the 32-year-old was excited by the prospect to compete in his first Grand Prix.

"For [the] race, lots to prepare to be honest," he added. "But today was [the] main focus to go through Q1, which was a shame for me, I had traffic in the last push lap.

"It was very [much a] shame but everything went well and I just need to focus for tomorrow on the race. Very excited for that."

title: Hamilton clinches first pole with Ferrari at Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton’s long wait for pole position with Ferrari finally came to an end in Qualifying at the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the Briton beating Mercedes’ George Russell by the smallest of margins.

An incredibly close battle for the top spot culminated in Hamilton’s spectacular final effort of 1m 16.514s, taking him to new heights as he claimed the 105th pole of his F1 career.

Russell missed out by just 0.009s as he led Charles Leclerc, Max Verstappen – who locked up on his last lap – and championship leader Kimi Antonelli, the top five separated by less than two-tenths.

McLaren’s immense pace from FP3 faded as Lando Norris wound up in P6, leading a frustrated Isack Hadjar who made an error that he struggled to bounce back from on his first effort in Q3.

Liam Lawson qualified P8 for Racing Bulls but will lose a position following his incident with Verstappen in FP2, as will the Dutchman. His team mate Arvid Lindblad will thus move from ninth to eighth, with Alpine’s Pierre Gasly rounding out the top 10.

The biggest shock of the session came in the form of Oscar Piastri’s Q2 elimination, with his high-pressure final lap not enough to warrant higher than P13 behind Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg (P11) and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto (P12).

Gabriel Bortoleto claimed 14th place in the second Audi from Ollie Bearman and Carlos Sainz, who outqualified his Williams team mate Alex Albon for the 14th time this season as the Briton settled for P17.

18th-placed Fernando Alonso joined him in being eliminated from Q1, having been ordered by Aston Martin to abandon the session due to a suspected water pressure issue linked to the ERS system.

Haas’ latest driver Ryo Hirakawa, who has replaced Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend in Mexico City, finished a respectable P19 in his first F1 Qualifying hour while Lance Stroll, Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas completed the order.

AS IT HAPPENED

Q1 – Hamilton sets the pace as Hirakawa misses out on Q2

Ferrari had looked like the strongest team during Friday’s running at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, but after Norris and Piastri delivered a strong result for McLaren in FP3, the battle for pole position once again looked wide open.

Amid pleasant conditions, the drivers began to file out on track when 18 minutes went on the clock for Q1, with crowd favourite Perez leading the way after he missed out on FP2 whilst Cadillac made a precautionary power unit change on his car.

Aston Martin’s Stroll was the first to suffer a big lock-up, the likes of which had impacted the majority in practice, and the frustration wasn’t over for the team yet as Alonso was instructed to stop the car on track. He did so on the run-off area in Estadio, prompting an immediate red flag that indicated an early end to his session.

Only half of the grid had completed their first flying lap with 11 minutes left, which meant that Hamilton topped the times with a 1m 18.249s ahead of Piastri and Alonso, mounting the pressure for those without an effort on the board.

Once the action resumed, Leclerc found himself in the P1 spot he had previously claimed in FP1 and FP2, followed closely by Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen and Russell. The other expected frontrunners of Piastri, Hamilton and Hadjar mingled further down the order, the latter having been affected by a lock-up.

It didn’t take long for the Aussie to capitalise on McLaren’s obvious pace and improve to P2, which soon became P3 when Hamilton came through as the next pace-setter, with times now in the 1m 17s bracket.

At the other end of the timing screen, Albon, Alonso – whose stoppage was made all the more devastating after his strong showing throughout practice – debutant Hirakawa, Stroll, Perez and Bottas were in the drop zone.

While the Haas driver was unable to progress from P19, Hadjar delivered an eye-catching lap to surge into second place, just 0.044s off Hamilton’s time. Leclerc settled for third in the opening segment, with Piastri and Russell rounding out the top five.

Knocked out: Albon, Alonso, Hirakawa, Stroll, Perez, Bottas

Q2 – Verstappen quickest but Piastri suffers shock exit

After a short reset, Q2 began and drivers were eager to get their banker laps in, which would be crucial if there were any further delays to the session. Piastri was among the first to do so as he posted a 1m 17.776s on the soft tyres, but his effort was eclipsed by Leclerc who went eight-tenths clear.

A stunning lap by Lindblad, whose earlier concerns around smoke in the cockpit seemed to have been resolved, sent him into P2 while further lock-ups for Norris and Hamilton left them at the tail end of the top 10.

As they unsurprisingly peeled into the pits for fresh tyres, Verstappen held the P1 time with a 1m 16.876s ahead of Leclerc, before Norris delivered the lap he needed to move out of the drop zone and into P3.

He left behind Gasly, Bortoleto, Bearman, Colapinto, Sainz and Hamilton, with Piastri another in need of a quicker lap as he lingered in P10, having abandoned an effort with just a few minutes remaining.

Although Hamilton avoided a surprise exit with a P3-worthy time, the same couldn’t be said for Piastri, who “had no rear grip” and was ultimately eliminated in P13 after failing to achieve any significant improvement. He therefore qualified behind Hulkenberg and Colapinto as Bortoleto, Bearman and Sainz were also excluded from Q3.

Knocked out: Hulkenberg, Colapinto, Piastri, Bortoleto, Bearman, Sainz

Q3 – Hamilton charges to maiden Ferrari pole

Piastri’s exit opened up a spot for Gasly to progress alongside both Racing Bulls and the usual suspects from the top four teams, but the question marks remained as to who would thrive in the final 12 minutes of Qualifying.

While some opted for prep laps, Ferrari got to business straightaway with Hamilton and Leclerc, the former setting a 1m 17.069s before his team mate charged into P1 with an advantage of more than four-tenths.

That earned him provisional pole, but would he cling onto it as the others executed their first runs? Although Norris initially came closest, Verstappen missed out by just 0.045s after Hadjar had gone wide and bailed out in the second Red Bull.

With knowledge of his one-place grid penalty on his mind, Verstappen stayed in the garage until the last possible moment whilst others set out on their final runs, which saw Russell leap into P1 with a superb lap.

However, Hamilton eked out a tiny margin of 0.009s to demote his former team mate to P2, and his time of 1m 16.514s proved to be unbeatable as Verstappen locked up when it mattered and ended in fourth place behind Leclerc.

“I hope you’re proud of yourselves too,” Hamilton told his team in an emotional radio message once his pole position was confirmed. “You’ve got to keep pushing. We’re on the right track but… woo! Such a good feeling.”

Antonelli, needing to finish ninth in Sunday’s Grand Prix to secure his maiden title, qualified fifth ahead of Norris, Hadjar, Lawson, Lindblad and Gasly.

Key quote

"Oh man, I'm lost for words," said polesitter Hamilton. "We've really done a good job with the set-up over the weekend. We've really worked, we've learned a lot from the last race. Wow, to have pole here, I mean, I don't even know if I've had a pole here before. So it feels special to be in Mexico and get that. My first, I think this is my first pole with Ferrari. And 105... I like that number."

title: Norris pips Antonelli to top spot in Mexico City FP3
excerpt:
Lando Norris finished fastest in Free Practice 3 ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, the McLaren driver just beating Kimi Antonelli and Charles Leclerc to the top spot.

The Briton posted a 1m 17.600s in the final minutes at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez on Saturday, leaving him just 0.001s clear of Antonelli, with Leclerc just one-tenth back.

Once the light went green at the end of the pit lane at 1130 local time Ryo Hirakawa immediately headed out, the Japanese driver replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas for the remainder of the weekend.

The Toyota World Endurance Championship driver had driven in FP1 on Friday and circulated frequently during the final hour of practice to gather vital data and experience ahead of his F1 debut.

Gabriel Bortoleto was another driver to venture out early on, but the Audi man immediately suffered a power unit issue with smoke coming from the back of his car as the Brazilian returned to the pits and failed to set a time.

Home hero Sergio Perez also failed to set a lap, Cadillac deciding to make a precautionary PU change on the Mexican's car ahead of Qualifying.

Antonelli, who stands on the cusp of claiming his maiden drivers' title this weekend, moved to the top of the times approaching the 20-minute mark with a 1m 18.754s on the medium Pirelli tyre, soon lowering the benchmark down a further tenth.

Times continued to tumble approaching the halfway point, Lewis Hamilton posting a 1m 18.268s before Ferrari team mate Leclerc registered a 1m 18.185s and then 1m 18.152s.

It took until less than 20 minutes remained for the leading runners to switch to the soft tyre and focus on outright one-lap pace, George Russell the first to make an attempt and setting a 1m 18.107s, stating "Turn 12 is so bad, there is no rear end".

Norris became the first driver to dip below the 1m 18s barrier, the reigning World Champion setting a 1m 17.873s, before Antonelli went top with a 1m 17.601s, and although Norris improved by a fraction, he still remained more than one-tenth adrift of Antonelli.

Leclerc backed out of his first attempt with the soft tyre after suffering a wide moment during the middle of the lap, eventually jumping up to second with another attempt after a strong final sector.

Drivers continued to exceed the limits, Hamilton suffering a moment of oversteer on the exit of the final corner, while Max Verstappen ran deep at Turn 4.

Norris went fastest in the closing minutes with a 1m 17.600s, just 0.001s clear of Antonelli, which remained fastest at the chequered flag.

Oscar Piastri (McLaren) was fourth behind Leclerc, with Red Bull's Verstappen, Hamilton, Russell, Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completing the top-10.

Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) was P11, from the Alpines of Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly, Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) and Ollie Bearman (Haas).

The order was completed by the Williams of Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, Lance Stroll (Aston Martin), Hirakawa and the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas.

title: Hirakawa to replace Ocon at Haas for Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
Haas have confirmed that Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Hirakawa – who has acted as a reserve driver for the squad since 2025 – participated in Free Practice 1 for the American outfit on Friday at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez before Ocon returned to action during the day’s second practice hour.

On Saturday morning, Haas announced that Hirakawa would take over driving duties for the rest of the weekend in Mexico.

A statement released by the team reads: “TGR Haas F1 Team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix, Saturday 31 October – Sunday 1 November.

“Hirakawa (32), a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship (2022, 2023) and 24 Hours of Le Mans winner (2022) with Toyota GAZOO Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October – his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall.

“The Japanese driver will partner team mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and Qualifying on Saturday and Sunday’s 71-lap Grand Prix – Hirakawa’s Formula 1 race debut.

“No further statements will be made at this time.”

title: Mekies predicts ‘one-off’ Mexico order in wind tunnel update
excerpt:
Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies believes the unique challenges of the Mexico City Grand Prix could shake up the competitive order, whilst also revealing when the team’s new wind tunnel is expected to become operational.

Speaking during Friday’s press conference following FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, Mekies acknowledged that Mexico City’s high altitude presents an unusual challenge for teams, with power unit performance and cooling requirements potentially playing a significant role in the weekend’s competitive order.

With the circuit located more than 2km above sea level, the thinner air creates additional demands on power units and chassis, forcing teams to make compromises to ensure reliability.

“I think there have been no unforeseen issues so far related to the altitude,” Mekies explained when asked if elevation had made any significant impacts on Red Bull's power unit.

“In fairness, we did have a PU issue with Isack [Hadjar] this morning and lost a bit of track time. The guys did a very good job and managed to send him back on track, but that was not linked with altitude.”

The Frenchman suggested that the conditions could lead to a different competitive picture compared to previous rounds, although he admitted it was too early to establish whether Red Bull would benefit.

“Both in terms of PU for the altitude and with all the compromises we are all having to make on the cooling side, we expect that this race could be a one-off in terms of pecking order.

“We don’t really have an idea whether we will have an advantage or a deficit this weekend. Only time will tell. But there is a fair amount of lap time, both on the PU side and the chassis side, that is in the game this weekend.”

Mekies reiterated that teams will need to balance performance against reliability, with the true impact of those compromises unlikely to become clear until later on in the weekend.

“In many respects everybody will not be operating at the optimum this weekend – PU side for the altitude, chassis side for the temperature. We are all ready to make some compromises to make sure our car can survive and our PU can survive in these conditions.”

Verstappen reacts to Lawson FP2 incident in Mexico

Mekies provides update on new Red Bull wind tunnel

Looking further ahead, Mekies also provided a long awaited update on Red Bull’s new wind tunnel, which is expected to replace the team’s ageing facility in Bedford.

The new state-of-the-art facility, which is being developed at Red Bull’s Milton Keynes headquarters, is an important step in the team’s longer-term development plans.

Mekies confirmed that the facility is expected to become operational at some point during 2027, with its impact more likely to be felt during the latter stages of development of next year’s car and throughout 2028.

“As much as the wind tunnel we are using has ultimately been producing extraordinary results over the last few years, it is most likely the oldest one on the grid,” he explained.

“As a result, if you jump to a state-of-the-art facility, of course you expect a competitive advantage from there. It’s not going to come as soon as we switch everything on, but it’s certainly going to unlock potential and give the talented people we have in the aero department another way to express their ideas.”

Asked about the timeline, Mekies added: “It's not ready yet. It’s something that will come online sometime during next season. Is it the first quarter, second quarter or third quarter? We will see. But it will be based on how much time we need to complete the calibration work and get it online first. So, it will most likely be for the second half of the 2027 car and hopefully for most of the 2028 car.”

The update follows comments from Max Verstappen, who has previously highlighted the limitations of the current facility.

Speaking to Viaplay in September, the four-time World Champion joked about the age of the existing equipment, comparing it to a wind tunnel “that comes from World War II”, before adding: “Of course you hope that as a team you can make a step there as well.”

Whilst Mekies acknowledged that improvements would not arrive immediately, he remains confident that the upgraded facility will offer Red Bull a competitive advantage as the teams looks to strengthen its position in the coming seasons.

title: Alonso cautiously upbeat after strong Friday in Mexico
excerpt:
With its long straights Mexico City wasn’t expected to be a strong venue for Aston Martin, but a solid performance on Friday has given the Silverstone team and their power unit partner Honda some cause for optimism.

Fernando Alonso was P7 in FP1, and while the position was not necessarily representative given the raft of rookies in the field and the problems suffered by various drivers, the 1.229s margin to pacesetter Charles Leclerc was at least promising.

In FP2 Alonso slipped back to P12 in the overall classification, but he moved closer to the front on lap time with a margin of just 0.769 to Leclerc – a huge improvement given that earlier in the season the gap was measured in seconds.

The AMR26 was benchmarked as the seventh fastest car, and the conclusion has to be that the package has thus far coped well with the challenges created by the high altitude in Mexico City.

The downside was a difficult day for the other car, with Jak Crawford stopping on track in FP1 and Lance Stroll playing catch-up in FP2.

Alonso admitted that so far the performance has exceeded expectations.

“Probably yes,” he said, when asked the question. “I was very open-minded coming to the weekend because Mexico is such a unique place with altitude and things, that I thought maybe we have a good surprise.

“At the moment at least on my side of the garage, the car is working well. I think Lance's car has some issues that they need to check for tomorrow.

“But part of the normal challenges in Mexico, with altitude, turbo speed, temperature, brakes, all these kinds of things that are a little bit on the limit. Apart from that, there are no big concerns into tomorrow.”

Alonso downplayed the challenge of low downforce levels: “No big difference, to be honest. We were all worrying about the lack of downforce this year compared to previous events, but I think the car feels very similar to the last few years here. So it was not an extra challenge, I would say."

Aston Martin’s Pedro de la Rosa suggested that the car is working well in the track’s many slow corners.

“It's fair to say it's slightly better than expected,” he noted. “Especially because I think probably the fact that there's a lot of low-speed component in this track, Sector 1, [Turns] 1, 2, 3, and 4, 5, 6 are very slow speed.

“Then you have the last sector, which is only mainly low-speed corners, second or first gear corners, which I think just makes us look a bit stronger. But anyway, it's still a challenge. Mexico will always be a challenge on temperatures, on the engine, on the braking. So we just have to manage that as well.”

Asked if the track could play to the strengths of an experienced driver like Alonso, de la Rosa added: “I think that from a physical point of view, there's no issues. So you have a long straight to actually catch up. There's not a lot of G forces. Also, the downforce you generate is quite low, because of the air density.

How 10 F1 rookies got on during FP1 in Mexico City

“But I think the fact that you are driving a car with very little downforce makes experienced drivers adapt faster. Also the fact that we have now two different sectors regarding asphalt means the drivers have to adapt a bit. You can push more on the last sector because there's more grip than on the first sector, which is the old asphalt.”

De la Rosa suggested that it was a good day on the power unit side.

“On the turbo lag, we haven't had many complaints from the drivers, which is positive,” he said. “So I think that Honda has done a very good job on the turbo lag, and minimising that effect.

“It's always an underlying factor, especially in a circuit like this at 2,200 metres. But it is mostly that we will have to manage engine cooling, brake cooling at a place like this. I think it's an overriding factor, rather than the turbo lag.”

title: Verstappen and Lawson get grid drops after ‘clumsy’ clash
excerpt:
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson have been given grid penalties by the stewards following their “unacceptable” and “clumsy” incident during second practice in Mexico.

The pair – having missed FP1 as rookies Ayumu Iwasa and Nikola Tsolov took over their cars – crossed paths in the early stages of FP2 when Verstappen made a move on Lawson into Turn 12.

Lawson tried to get back ahead at the following left-hand turn through the stadium section, with Verstappen bouncing over the kerb on the exit and rejoining alongside the New Zealander, causing damage to the Red Bull’s floor and Racing Bulls’ front wing.

A red flag was thrown to recover the debris, and both drivers picked up their practice programmes – Verstappen finishing P5 and Lawson P9.

After the session, the stewards reviewed video footage and data, as well as speaking to Verstappen and Lawson, before issuing individual one-place grid drops.

“On the approach to Turn 12, Car 3 [Verstappen] was on a preparation lap and Car 30 [Lawson] was on a cool down lap preparing for another push lap,” read the stewards’ decision document. “The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the stewards particularly in view of the warning that had been given at the Team Managers meeting earlier this day.

“Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and ‘clumsy’.

“Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years.”

Speaking after FP2, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane had also used the word “unnecessary” to describe Verstappen and Lawson’s coming together.

“I think one word, just ‘unnecessary’ in a practice session; completely unnecessary, and I say that to both of them,” commented Permane, after Verstappen criticised Lawson for “not very smart behaviour”.

"I don’t know what Max has said, I haven’t heard anything, but I’m sure he’s got his opinion and I’m sure Liam has got his opinion. Mine is it’s just not needed, and they can both do better.”

Verstappen and Lawson were also given a penalty point apiece by the stewards.

title: Breaking: Liam Lawson at risk of Mexico City qualifying disqualification
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is at risk of being disqualified from qualifying at this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, following a potential technical infraction.

The New Zealander had superbly qualified in eighth at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, however, shortly after the session his car was referred to the stewards by FIA technical delegate Jo Bauer.

According to Bauer's report: "Car 30, driver Liam Lawson, was in breach of the minimum MGU-K power requirement just after crossing the line on his fastest lap in Q2 at 15:47:36.

"This is a breach of Articles C5.12.6 and C5.12.7. The driver maximum power demand and the electrical DC power of the ERS-K were reduced at greater rates than what is permitted by the regulations."

If Lawson's car is found to have breached the regulations, the likely outcome will be a disqualification from the session, promoting Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad onto the fourth row.

title: Kimi Antonelli admits for first time to feeling weight of F1 title history
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has conceded for the first time to feeling "tense" as F1 drivers' title history beckons for the 20-year-old.

Mercedes driver Antonelli will start the Mexico City Grand Prix from fourth on the grid at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez, up one position after finishing fifth quickest due to four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen serving a one-place penalty after his on-track altercation with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson during second practice.

Although the scenario for Antonelli appears to be a straightforward one going into the race, needing to finish ninth or higher, even if Mercedes' team-mate George Russell - who starts second - wins the race, the magnitude of what he could achieve now sits heavy upon him.

Asked as to how he would sleep tonight knowing the magnitude of what awaits him, the young Italian replied: "It hasn't been the easiest weekend, to be fair, and definitely still not feeling 100 per cent.

"But, as well, the thought of what could happen is there, and I'm definitely a bit more tense than usual. I definitely don't feel as relaxed, but I will try to get a good sleep and then focus on tomorrow."

Antonelli conceded that qualifying was not his best, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton on pole - the seven-time F1 champion's first for over three years - followed by Russell and then the second SF-26 of Charles Leclerc.

"I struggled to get a good feeling with the tyres in Q3, and I just didn't have the most confidence," said Antonelli.

"I was a bit tense, not gonna lie, and yeah, it was a poor lap. You know, many mistakes here and there.

"But overall, still P4 and a lot to play for."

title: Esteban Ocon makes statement after reports of violence behind Haas axe
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon has denied that any physical altercation took place between him and any member of the Haas team after being dropped from this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Haas confirmed on Friday that Ryo Hirakawa would replace Ocon for the remainder of the event, having withdrawn him from the car without disclosing an official cause. The team said only that the Frenchman's absence was not down to illness.

The sudden switch triggered a wave of speculation, with reports linking Ocon's benching to a heated radio exchange with race engineer Laura Mueller during second practice over a mandated tyre strategy change from soft to medium compounds.

Other reports went further, alleging a paddock confrontation between Ocon and team principal Ayao Komatsu.

Komatsu himself declined to discuss internal details when asked, refusing to confirm or deny whether the practice dispute was behind the decision to sideline his driver.

Ocon, though, has now issued a statement addressing the speculation directly, rejecting suggestions that violence played any part in the dispute.

"Following the recent decision from Haas F1 Team confirming that I will not be participating in this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, I wish to formally address some media reports and speculation surrounding the situation," Ocon said.

"Last night, a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved. Whilst I acknowledge that this took place, I categorically reject any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature.

"I strongly condemn violence in all its forms and firmly believe that disagreements should always be handled with professionalism, respect, and mutual understanding.

"I kindly ask that speculation be avoided while the matter is being addressed.

"Further updates will be communicated in due course."

title: Lewis Hamilton 'lost for words' after landing major Ferrari milestone
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was left "lost for words" after claiming pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix, his first pole for Ferrari.

It was Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc who entered qualifying arguably as the favourite, having topped first and second practice.

Hamilton's route to the final part of qualifying was far from smooth, with a mistake on his first lap in Q2 leaving the veteran needing a big lap to avoid an embarrassing exit.

He navigated the tricky situation but then delivered a disappointing opening lap at the start of Q3. However, fitted with new soft tyres, Hamilton unlocked exceptional pace right at the death of qualifying.

The 41-year-old denied George Russell pole by just 0.009s to become the oldest pole-sitter since Mario Andretti at the 1982 Italian Grand Prix, while also extending his own record for the most poles in F1.

Hamilton was elated after securing pole at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, particularly as he moved on to another career milestone.

"That felt great! That feels good!" said Hamilton. "I'm so happy. I'm lost for words. It's been a really challenging weekend.

"FP1 we had an [aero] rake running and an engine issue yesterday, which meant we were on the back foot and I didn't get to do a long run.

"But we've done a really good job with the setup. We learned a lot from the last race. It's so close between us all. For example, in Q2, I didn't get my lap in at the beginning.

"I think the others have a new tyre for the start but to have pole here. It feels special to be here in Mexico and [pole position] 105, I like that number."

How Lewis Hamilton continues to push at 41

Claiming an F1 pole at 41 years old is a remarkable achievement for Hamilton, who recently hinted that he could continue until he is 44 in order to enter the African Grand Prix in Rwanda.

The hunger and determination as not gone from the Ferrari driver, who expressed after securing pole how he continues to push on.

"When there’s a will there’s a way! It’s all in the mind for all of us. You might feel aches and pains, luckily I don’t," added Hamilton.

"I spar a lot and do all those different things you do to try to keep yourself young and fit but I love what I do. That love is not gone. I wake up every day thinking about it, I dream about it.

"I’ve got this amazing support around the world. These guys keep me going, so I hope they’re happy with that today and I hope I can deliver for them tomorrow."

title: Lewis Hamilton defies age barrier to end three-year wait for pole position
excerpt:
Finally, Lewis Hamilton! Finally!

Lewis Hamilton finally ended his long pole drought by securing the top spot on the grid for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

It was pole position 105 for F1's record holder, with his 104th at the Hungarian Grand Prix over three years ago.

At 41, Ferrari driver Hamilton is also the oldest driver on pole position since Mario Andretti in the 1982 Italian Grand Prix.

Hamilton produced a brilliant flying final lap, and despite many of his rivals coming at him later in the session, his lap of one minute 16.514s was enough to beat Mercedes' George Russell by nine-thousandths of a second.

Charles Leclerc, who had looked favourite over Hamilton to secure top spot, will start third ahead of champion-in-waiting Kimi Antonelli.

The 20-year-old Italian was actually fifth quickest, but moves up a place due to a one-place grid penalty for Max Verstappen after an on-track altercation with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in FP2 on Friday.

McLaren's Lando Norris lines up sixth ahead of Isack Hadjar in his Red Bull, followed by Racing Bulls teammates Arvid Lindblad and Lawson - the duo trading places due to the New Zealander also serving a one-place penalty - with Alpine's Pierre Gasly 10th.

[Article continues below]

Lewis Hamilton defies age barrier to end three-year wait for pole position

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Poor Piastri misery

Oscar Piastri and McLaren suffered a rare disaster in Q2, leaving the Australian lining up in a lowly 13th on the grid.

Despite plenty of fresh soft tyres available, McLaren gambled by running Piastri and Norris on used softs for their first runs in the 15-minute session. Piastri's lap was naturally not good enough.

On new softs for the second run, Piastri made an error in the middle sector, forcing him to abort. After a cool-down lap, his second attempt saw him fall almost four-tenths of a second shy of reaching Q3.

"I don't know what happened," said Piastri over team radio. "I had no rear grip." To rub salt into the wounds, Norris set the fastest lap of the session, almost a second quicker.

Ahead of Piastri on the grid will be Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Franco Colapinto in his Alpine in 11th and 12th, whilst behind him will be Oliver Bearman for Haas and Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will line up 14th and 15th.

Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto was 14th fastest, but drops five places due to a power unit penalty.

Sainz, meanwhile, is under investigation by the stewards for failing to follow the race director's instructions, specifically relating to the escape road.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

More Aston Martin and Cadillac misery

The first part of qualifying was disrupted by a red flag shown with 11 minutes remaining, due to a suspected water pressure issue linked to the ERS, for Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso that resulted in him stopping in the stadium section, sparking a seven-minute delay.

Although Alonso said over the radio he was close to the pit entry, the command of "Stop the car now! Stop the car now!" was unequivocal, sparking frustration from Alonso, who slapped his hands against the AMR26's steering wheel when he stopped.

Alonso's time of 1:18.908s, which left him third on the timesheet when the session was halted, was only good enough for 18th by the time it ended. Alonso was also noted for 'general safety' by the stewards as he did not fit the steering wheel back on his car, eventually earning a reprimand.

Alonso will have Williams' Alex Albon ahead of him, whilst behind will be Haas rookie Ryo Hirakawa, drafted in on Saturday morning after the team announced Esteban Ocon would take no further part in the weekend, stating only it was not through illness.

With Bortoleto 19th, Aston Martin's Lance Stroll will start 20th, whilst the Cadillac pair of home hero Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas will be on the back row, the duo separated by three-quarters of a second, adding further pressure on the Finn to retain his seat for next season.

Bottas also starts with a meaningless 50-place grid penalty due to a complete power unit change. Perez sat out all but one lap of FP3 with a PU problem that necessitated a change in the interval, albeit one from the pool, so avoiding a penalty like his teammate.

title: F1 rookie reveals bizarre impairment: 'I couldn't feel my legs'
excerpt:
Nikola Tsolov has explained the strange issue he suffered during the first practice session for the Mexico City Grand Prix, as he momentarily lost feeling in his legs.

The Bulgarian driver made his first appearance at a grand prix weekend on Friday, standing in for Liam Lawson at Racing Bulls.

The outing came as he seeks to convince the team that he should be selected for a full-time drive next year.

During the session, cameras spotted Tsolov standing up in the cockpit when he returned to the garage after reporting that he was "losing circulation" in his right leg.

Speaking after the session, Tsolov revealed that it is something that has happened before in F2.

"I had that a few times before, driving in F2," Tsolov said. "It's just the seat being a bit tighter than what we would like on my right leg. My blood flow stopped.

"When you press in full throttle, you move up into the seat. That kind of compresses your legs.

"That was the thing; I couldn't feel them. It was a dead leg, pretty much.

"You know when you get the tingly feeling, with pins and needles. That was it in the beginning, and I thought, 'I will do that; it's fine'.

"But at some point I stopped feeling my legs, so I had to jump out. I had to shake it out, and after two or three minutes, it came back."

[Article continues below]

Tsolov felt 'ready' for FP1 debut despite lack of F1 mileage

Tsolov is currently contending for the F2 title, sitting seven points adrift of championship leader Rafael Camara with two rounds remaining.

Tsolov is under serious consideration for a drive at Racing Bulls next year, despite the strong performances of both Lawson and rookie team-mate Arvid Lindblad.

The FP1 appearance for Tsolov saw the 19-year-old complete 28 laps, with his best effort just over one-tenth down on Lindblad's time.

Despite his lack of preparation ahead of his FP1 debut, Tsolov insisted he felt ready for the outing.

"I did one TPC (testing of previous cars) day with last year's car in Imola back in August,” he said.

"Then I did a day and a half of sim around two weeks ago with the team in Faenza, and that's about it. That was my preparation.

"I was ready for it. To be honest, I didn't really think about it too much. I didn't really stress it, so I managed to arrive in a calm mental state."

title: Jack Doohan unexpectedly on the brink of huge F1 opportunity
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa is stepping into Esteban Ocon's Haas for the Mexico City Grand Prix. But it is far from certain that he will see out the rest of the F1 season in the car.

Haas caused a stir on Saturday by announcing that Ocon would take no further part in the remainder of the race weekend in Mexico. The team gave no reason for the sudden switch, although it confirmed that Ocon is not ill.

Hirakawa takes over the seat from the third practice session onwards, marking his official Formula 1 debut.

As to the remainder of the season, whilst a return for Ocon looks to be ruled out, Hirakawa is not Haas' regular third driver.

The Japanese was present in Mexico this weekend as reserve and took part in first practice, but Haas already faces a potential headache for next week's São Paulo Grand Prix.

Hirakawa is expected in Monza for the final round of the World Endurance Championship. The 32-year-old races for Toyota, one of Haas' major sponsors.

That opens the door for a recall for Jack Doohan, who is the expected reserve for Brazil and the races that follow in Las Vegas and the Middle East double-header in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Doohan, who started 2025 as Alpine's race driver, lost his seat to Franco Colapinto after only six races. The Australian then came close to landing a permanent seat at Haas.

F1 paddock sources have told RacingNews365 that the Australian made a strong impression during the American outfit's TPC testing, only for the team to opt for Rafael Camara as Ocon's replacement from next season.

[Article continues below]

Rafael Camara held back?

With Ocon's earlier-than-planned exit from Haas, some have suggested giving Camara a chance before his official debut in 2027. But the prevailing view in the paddock is that it would be too early to throw the Brazilian in at the deep end.

It could also harm his prospects heading into next season, especially since he is still fighting for the F2 title, with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi still to come.

Haas therefore has another puzzle to solve before the season concludes. Hirakawa gets his chance now, a move that will undoubtedly please Toyota, given the driver's status as one of the Japanese manufacturer's prized assets.

But the odds remain strong that it will be a one-off appearance, with Doohan set to be back in the car next weekend.

title: Max Verstappen doubles down on Liam Lawson criticism: 'That doesn't happen to me'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has refused to back down in his criticism of Liam Lawson following their on-track spat in second practice for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Verstappen and Lawson both found themselves in front of the stewards at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez after the session and handed one-place grid penalties for a collision described as "unacceptable".

Both drivers suffered damage to their cars, with four-time F1 champion Verstappen losing a piece of the bargeboard on his RB22, whilst Lawson sustained front-wing damage to his Racing Bulls as they came together in the stadium complex after running wheel-to-wheel in the build-up.

Immediately after the incident, Verstappen turned on Lawson, pointing an accusing finger, stating that, "For me, it's just not very smart behaviour."

Speaking to Viaplay after the final practice session, Verstappen still felt disappointed in the New Zealander, even though both were deemed at fault by the stewards.

"Look, you’re fighting for your seat, so you definitely shouldn’t be picking a fight with me,” said Verstappen.

"I’ve always supported him. I get along with him very well, and I’ve always spoken very positively about him within the team."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen to Lawson - 'Just think logically'

Referring to what happened to Lawson last year when he was demoted to Racing Bulls after just two grands prix as Verstappen's team-mate at Red Bull, Verstappen added: "Of course, it sucked for him last year.

"I think it’s really unfortunate when something like that happens. I’m really not a difficult person.

"When I put on my helmet, I always try to get the most out of it, but not in practice

"I just won’t let anyone push me off the track. That doesn’t happen to me."

Verstappen claims he has learned important lessons at Red Bull that drivers in the 'sister' team should also heed.

"When you are in the same family, you're always taught that you have to have a lot of respect for the A-team," he said.

"I didn't do this at Toro Rosso [what Lawson did]. You don't go driving the Red Bull drivers off the track; you just don't do that."

Offering Lawson a piece of advice, he concluded: "Just think logically about the situation you are in."

title: Lando Norris pips Kimi Antonelli as Mexico FP3 serves up an unexpected curveball
excerpt:
Lando Norris sent a statement by topping the third free practice session at the Mexico City Grand Prix, putting in the fastest time of the weekend so far.

Remarkably, he pipped Kimi Antonelli at the post by just a thousandth of a second, with a 1:17.600.

Charles Leclerc was third at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, with Oscar Piastri and Max Verstappen rounding out the top five.

Ryo Hirakawa, who is racing for Haas in place of Esteban Ocon, finished FP3 in P19, almost six tenths and four places off team-mate Ollie Bearman.

Gabriel Bortoleto managed just two laps before problems struck his side of the Audi garage, not for the first time this weekend, and Sergio Perez could muster just one; a nightmare scenario heading into qualifying on Halloween.

First half

FP3 kicked off in characteristically slow fashion, although there were immediate runners, with many drivers looking to make up for lost time.

Be it due to relinquishing their car for FP1, reliability issues or replacing Ocon, the Audis, Alpines and Hirakawa made their way onto the circuit.

Nico Hulkenberg set the early pace with a 1:20.572, some time off a representative effort, but Bortoleto was experiencing issues with his R26.

It has been a messy weekend for the German marque, after multiple indiscretions on Friday, and the power unit problems that plagued its early part of the season appeared to have resurfaced.

Similarly to before FP2, Audi confirmed there was a technical issue that was being investigated. It ultimately ended his session almost immediately.

As the lap times started to tumble, Pierre Gasly moved to the head of the pack, ahead of Arvid Lindblad.

But 20 minutes in, the leading teams started to find their groove, with Antonelli and George Russell bringing the lap times into the 1:18s.

Leclerc continued his impressive form from the opening two hours of practice, going top with a 1:18.720, only to be quickly displaced by Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton, before finding another five tenths of lap time to reclaim the advantage.

The supremacy of the Ferrari was evident, with his team-mate edging 23 milliseconds ahead as the session hit the half-hour mark.

Final 30 minutes

The yo-yo'ing at the top of the timing board between the two Ferraris continued as the clock approached 25 minutes remaining.

Leclerc went a hundredth of a second quicker than Hamilton with a 1:18.152, but that time was still some way off the more representative FP2 session, which ended in the 1:17.8s.

Meanwhile, Antonelli and Hadjar had the measure of their more experienced team-mates in third and fourth, with Russell and Verstappen down in seventh and eighth, with both McLarens between them.

Hirakawa, back in the car for the second time this weekend, was running in P14, five places and almost seven tenths ahead of Ollie Bearman.

Down at Cadillac, things were not going well. The team confirmed that a precautionary power unit change was being undertaken on Perez's car. The home hero, like Bortoleto, was without a time on the board with just 15 minutes to run.

Whilst medium tyres had dominated the first three-quarters of an hour, it was time for the soft, red-walled Pirellis.

Antonelli went first, but could not topple the Ferraris. Russell, however, had no such issues, setting a 1:18.107 to go to fastest.

But soon, Norris resumed his quietly assured weekend to beat his compatriot, whilst Piastri filed in behind.

On the verge of F1 championship glory, Antonelli was keen to send a message. His 1:17.601 marked the quickest time of the round.

However, Norris had other ideas, going faster by just a millisecond to top the final free practice session before qualifying.

title: Haas team principal takes clear stance over Esteban Ocon furore
excerpt:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu refused to shed any light on why Esteban Ocon had been replaced for this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Haas caused uproar in the paddock on Saturday morning when it announced that reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa would replace Ocon for the remainder of the weekend at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez.

No reason was given, only confirming that Ocon's absence was not due to illness, sparking feverish speculation behind the team's decision.

Komatsu's appearance as the designated team principal offering opinions and thoughts on the sessions for Sky Sports F1 offered an opportunity for the matter to be clarified as final practice unfolded.

Komatsu, though, remained tight-lipped.

Asked simply to explain why there was no Ocon, Komatsu replied: "I can't tell you much, but at least I can tell you that he's not ill. That's as much I can tell you."

Suggested to Komatsu that Ocon's energised state on the radio during FP2 over the team's run plan may have played a part in his axing this weekend, the Japanese said: "No, I'm sorry, but I can't go into any details."

Looking ahead to next weekend's São Paulo GP and what could unfold, with Hirakawa competing at Monza in the World Endurance Championship for Toyota, and so unavailable, Komatsu said: "Honestly, the only thing I can say is we are focused on what's right in front of us, so trying to get Ryo in the best shape for quali this afternoon."

Pressed on whether Hirakawa's absence caused a problem, and whether another reserve would be drafted in, Komatsu signed off by saying, "Again, I've not got there yet. I'm really just focusing on this session right now."

title: Isack Hadjar learns stewards' verdict after paddock altercation with fan
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has avoided a sanction following an altercation with a fan on Friday in Mexico.

A video circulating on social media on Friday evening showed Hadjar being approached by a fan who sought to take a photo with the Frenchman.

Hadjar appeared disinterested in doing so and extended his arm to keep the fan at bay as he journeyed towards the Red Bull garage.

However, the video then showed Hadjar appearing to push the fan with his right arm before continuing to walk on.

The altercation caught the attention of the stewards, who summoned Hadjar to a hearing on Saturday afternoon.

Hadjar has been given a formal warning by the stewards.

The stewards felt there were extenuating circumstances at the time as to why Hadjar should not receive a serious punishment.

A statement read: "The driver stated that he was running late for FP1 and had stopped to have a photograph with a young fan, when he was approached by a paddock guest in an aggressive manner.

"One security person was walking behind him and was unable to intervene and prevent what was tantamount to an invasion of the driver’s private space.

"The driver initially resisted the move by placing his hand on the waist of the guest, holding him at bay, then the driver pushed him aside with his open right hand.

"This latter action by the driver is regarded as a breach of the regulations, however, in mitigation of penalty the stewards considered the following matters (in accordance with the guidelines provided in Appendix B of the FIA International Sporting Code):

"a) The driver was reacting to an uninvited and rather aggressive action by another person.

"b) The driver was endeavouring to make his way to the start of FP1 through a congested area.

"c) The driver did not have sufficient security present.

"d) The guest was invading his personal space without his consent.

"e) The general issue drivers have experienced moving through the paddock."

title: Who is Haas F1 driver Ryo Hirakawa, the shock Esteban Ocon replacement?
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa is set to make his Formula 1 race debut at the Mexico City Grand Prix after Haas announced the Japanese driver would replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend.

Haas has confirmed that reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, handing the Japanese driver his long-awaited F1 race debut.

The 32-year-old will partner Oliver Bearman in final practice, qualifying and Sunday's race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Hirakawa is already familiar with the VF-26, having driven the car during Friday's opening practice session, finishing 15th before Ocon returned for FP2.

Haas has not provided a reason for the unexpected change, leaving questions surrounding Ocon's absence. However, the team did not confirm it is not because of illness.

Although Hirakawa has never started an F1 grand prix, he brings considerable experience from other categories, having won multiple world championship titles and the prestigious 24 Hours of Le Mans.

[Article continues below]

Who is Ryo Hirakawa?

Born in Hiroshima, Japan, on 7 March 1994, Hirakawa began his motorsport career in karting before progressing through the Japanese single-seater ranks.

He won the Japanese Formula 3 Championship in 2012, the same year he secured the Porsche Carrera Cup Japan title.

His performances helped him progress into Super Formula in 2013, where he established himself as a regular frontrunner.

Hirakawa enjoyed his strongest Super Formula campaign in 2020, finishing runner-up in the championship, and claimed four victories during his time in the series.

He also achieved success in Japan's Super GT championship, winning the GT500 title in 2017 with TOM'S.

However, his greatest achievements have come in international endurance racing.

In 2022, Hirakawa joined Toyota's leading World Endurance Championship programme, sharing the manufacturer's No. 8 car with former F1 drivers Sebastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley.

The trio won the 24 Hours of Le Mans that year before securing the World Endurance Championship drivers' title.

They successfully defended their championship in 2023, establishing Hirakawa as one of Toyota's most successful endurance racing drivers.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

How did Hirakawa become involved in F1?

Despite spending much of his career competing in Japan and endurance racing, Hirakawa has gained experience with several F1 teams.

He joined McLaren as a reserve driver in 2024, undertaking simulator and testing duties before making his official F1 practice debut at that year's Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Hirakawa subsequently joined Alpine as a test and reserve driver for 2025, taking part in opening practice at his home grand prix in Japan.

However, his association with the French manufacturer was short-lived.

In April 2025, he switched to Haas as the American outfit strengthened its technical relationship with Toyota.

The partnership provided Hirakawa with further opportunities to drive F1 machinery, including four practice appearances during the 2025 season.

He retained his reserve driver role for 2026 while continuing to compete for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship.

Hirakawa has participated in three FP1 sessions for Haas this season, including Friday's outing in Mexico City, providing him with experience of the current machinery ahead of his unexpected promotion.

[Article continues below]

Why is Hirakawa replacing Ocon?

Haas has not explained its decision to replace Ocon midway through the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

The Frenchman returned to the car for second practice on Friday, finishing 13th after Hirakawa had completed the opening session.

Ocon was involved in a tense radio exchange with race engineer Laura Mueller during FP2 over tyre strategy, although there is no confirmed connection between the exchange and Haas' subsequent decision.

The 30-year-old is already set to leave the team at the end of the season, with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara due to replace him in 2027.

Hirakawa's promotion comes against that backdrop, although Haas has only confirmed the change for the remainder of the Mexico City weekend.

For Hirakawa, the announcement presents an opportunity to make his first grand prix start after years of competing at the highest levels of Japanese and endurance racing.

At 32, he will become one of the oldest drivers to make his F1 debut in the modern era when he takes to the grid on Sunday, younger than only Andre Lotterer, who made his debut for Caterham at the Belgian Grand Prix in 2014.

title: Haas share more information on sudden Esteban Ocon withdrawal
excerpt:
The reason Esteban Ocon is missing the rest of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix is not because of illness, Haas has confirmed.

The American team has not stated the cause of Ocon's withdrawal at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez and has no plans to make any further announcements at this time.

Multiple drivers have needed to miss press duties over the weekend thus far due to illness, with Kimi Antonelli and Valtteri Bottas being excused from media day.

Sergio Perez, celebrating his 300th grand prix start in front of his home crowd, was also permitted to be absent from his own press obligations on Saturday.

Therefore, it was pertinent to establish that Ocon is not also sick.

The Frenchman has been replaced by reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the remainder of the round, starting with FP3. The 32-year-old rookie has taken part in numerous FP1 sessions before, including earlier in the weekend, in place of Ocon.

The one-time grand prix winner will not continue with the Ayao Komatsu-led squad in 2027, after two years at the team.

Given the partnership is ending, there have been suggestions of internal tensions between Ocon and Haas, but it is unclear if his unexpected withdrawal is a result of that relationship further breaking down or if it is because of a different reason, like a family matter.
